summary:
I developed Orbital Horizon 2026 — 3D Space Mission Architect, an interactive 3D spaceflight sandbox where players design, launch, and pilot custom spacecraft across the solar system.
How It Addresses the Challenge:
Instead of keeping aerospace concepts abstract, the game puts students in charge of the complete mission lifecycle. Inside the 3D Vehicle Assembly Building, players engineer multi-stage rockets from 21 modular parts while balancing competing constraints—budgets, mass, thrust-to-weight ratios (TWR > 1.02), center-of-mass alignment, net power, and communications range (up to 2.0 AU). Players then fly their designs across 28 missions (Earth orbit, Moon, Venus, and Mars) or free-flight mode, using an Orbital Flight Computer, 360° navball, and transfer maps to see how each choice affects mission success.
Why It Is Important:
By turning orbital mechanics and systems engineering into a hands-on "build anything, go anywhere" experience, Orbital Horizon 2026 bridges classroom theory and real-world aerospace problem-solving. It lets students experiment safely, learn from failure, and master the real trade-offs behind space exploration
details:
Project details : 1. What does it do, and how does it work?

Orbital Horizon 2026 is an interactive 3D spaceflight sandbox where players design, launch, and pilot custom spacecraft across the solar system. Players begin in the 3D Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB), assembling multi-stage rockets from 21 modular parts across Command, Engines, Fuel, Science, Power/Comms, and Landing categories. Once built, players launch from Pad 39A into a real-time orbital physics simulation. Using a 360° navball, multi-stage decoupling, an Orbital Flight Computer, and interplanetary transfer maps, players navigate atmospheric layers, achieve orbit, and fly across 28 guided missions (spanning Earth, the Moon, Venus, and Mars) or explore freely in sandbox mode with up to 1000x time warp.

2. What benefits does it have?

• Hands-On Systems Thinking: Replaces passive textbook learning with active trial-and-error engineering.
• Risk-Free Experimentation: Allows students to test wild prototypes, experience real failure modes (like low thrust or power loss), and iterate quickly using a 20% cash-back part recycling system.
• True Sandbox Replayability: Combines 28 structured historical and 2026-era missions with an open-ended "build anything, go anywhere" free-flight mode.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project aims to make complex aerospace engineering and orbital mechanics accessible, intuitive, and exciting for students. By letting learners manage an entire mission from blueprint to touchdown, it bridges the gap between classroom physics theory and real-world space mission architecture, inspiring the next generation of STEM innovators.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

• Development Environment & Software: Built using [e.g., Google AI Studio / Three.js / Unity / WebGL] and [e.g., Visual Studio Code / Blender for 3D modeling].
• Coding Languages: Developed with [e.g., JavaScript / TypeScript / HTML5 / CSS3 / C#].
• Hardware: Developed and tested on [e.g., standard student laptops / desktop PCs with integrated or dedicated graphics], optimized to run smoothly in a web browser without needing high-end gaming hardware.

5. How is your project creative?

Instead of forcing players down a single scripted path, Orbital Horizon 2026 blends realistic aerospace diagnostics—such as Center of Mass (CoM) vs. Center of Thrust (CoT) alignment, Sphere of Influence (SOI) transitions, and Delta-v calculations—with total sandbox freedom. Features like the built-in Mission Academy, real-time telemetry HUD, and multi-scale solar system maps turn invisible mathematical concepts into visual, interactive gameplay.

6. What factors did your team consider?

• Realism vs. Accessibility: Balancing authentic orbital physics (TWR > 1.02, atmospheric drag, 2.0 AU comms range) with intuitive controls, automated pre-launch diagnostics, and time warp so beginners aren't overwhelmed.
• Competing Engineering Trade-Offs: Designing the 21 parts so every addition forces meaningful compromises between payload mass, fuel capacity, electrical power, communications range, and mission budget.
• Performance & Usability: Ensuring smooth 3D rendering, clear visual telemetry, and responsive flight controls across standard student devices
